items.title: Portable timekeeping
items.text: Clockmakers in Nuremberg, among them Peter Henlein, make small spring-driven clocks that can be carried, the ancestors of the watch.

items.title: The pendulum clock
items.text: Christiaan Huygens patents the pendulum clock, making clocks accurate to seconds rather than minutes.

items.title: The balance spring
items.text: Huygens applies a spiral balance spring to the balance wheel, the single biggest leap in portable accuracy.

items.title: The lever escapement
items.text: Thomas Mudge invents the detached lever escapement, which still ticks inside nearly every mechanical watch.

items.title: Harrison's H4
items.text: John Harrison's marine timekeeper H4 is tested at sea, solving the problem of longitude.

items.title: Self-winding
items.text: Abraham-Louis Perrelet builds a self-winding "perpétuelle" pocket watch powered by the wearer's motion.

items.title: The tourbillon
items.text: Abraham-Louis Breguet patents the tourbillon, a rotating cage that averages out positional errors caused by gravity.

items.title: The first wristwatch
items.text: Breguet is commissioned to make a bracelet watch for Caroline Murat, Queen of Naples, one of the earliest wristwatches recorded.

items.title: Patek founded
items.text: Antoine Norbert de Patek and François Czapek begin making watches in Geneva; Adrien Philippe joins in 1845.

items.title: The Santos
items.text: Louis Cartier designs a wristwatch for the aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont so he can read the time without letting go of the controls.

items.title: Automatic wristwatch
items.text: John Harwood patents a self-winding wristwatch with a swinging weight.

items.title: The Oyster
items.text: Rolex patents the Oyster, a hermetically sealed case. In 1927 Mercedes Gleitze wears one while swimming the English Channel.

items.title: The Perpetual rotor
items.text: Rolex introduces the 360° Perpetual rotor, the template for modern automatic winding.

items.title: The dive watch
items.text: The Blancpain Fifty Fathoms and the Rolex Submariner define the modern dive watch.

items.title: Electric 500
items.text: Hamilton launches the Electric 500, the first battery-powered wristwatch.

items.title: The Speedmaster
items.text: Omega introduces the Speedmaster, a racing chronograph that would later go to the Moon.

items.title: Accutron
items.text: Bulova releases the Accutron, regulated by a tuning fork vibrating at 360 Hz and guaranteed to within a minute a month.

items.title: Flight-qualified
items.text: After brutal testing, NASA qualifies the Omega Speedmaster for its crewed space missions.

items.title: On the Moon
items.text: Buzz Aldrin wears his Speedmaster on the lunar surface during Apollo 11.

items.title: Seiko Astron
items.text: Seiko sells the Astron 35SQ in Tokyo, the world's first quartz wristwatch. The quartz revolution begins.

items.title: The automatic chronograph race
items.text: Zenith's El Primero, the Heuer-Breitling-Hamilton Calibre 11 and Seiko's 6139 all bring automatic chronographs to market.

items.title: The LED watch
items.text: Hamilton shows the Pulsar prototype, the first electronic digital watch. It goes on sale in 1972.

items.title: Royal Oak
items.text: Audemars Piguet unveils the Royal Oak, designed by Gérald Genta: a steel luxury sports watch.

items.title: Six-digit LCD
items.text: Seiko introduces the 06LC, the first watch with a six-digit liquid-crystal display.

items.title: Solar quartz
items.text: Citizen launches the Crystron Solar Cell, the first light-powered analog quartz watch. The same year, Patek Philippe releases the Nautilus.

items.title: Swatch and G-Shock
items.text: Swatch launches its plastic quartz watches and helps save the Swiss industry; Casio launches the first G-Shock, the DW-5000C.

items.title: Auto-quartz
items.text: Seiko launches the AGS, later called Kinetic: a quartz watch charged by a rotor.

items.title: Lange returns
items.text: Walter Lange and Günter Blümlein refound A. Lange & Söhne in Glashütte after German reunification.

items.title: Radio-controlled
items.text: Junghans releases the Mega 1, the first radio-controlled wristwatch, synchronising itself with an atomic clock signal.

items.title: Co-axial and Spring Drive
items.text: Omega launches the first serial-production co-axial escapement (George Daniels' invention), and Seiko launches Spring Drive.

items.title: Silicon
items.text: Ulysse Nardin's Freak uses silicon escapement parts, beginning the silicon era.

items.title: GPS solar
items.text: Seiko launches the Astron GPS Solar, which sets itself by satellite anywhere on Earth.

items.title: Apple Watch
items.text: The Apple Watch goes on sale, and within a few years smartwatches outsell the entire Swiss industry by volume.

items.title: MoonSwatch
items.text: The Omega × Swatch Bioceramic MoonSwatch launches to queues around the world, bringing a new generation into watches.
